tagline: A former toll road crosses mountains once contested by Civil War armies.
intro: The Staunton-Parkersburg Turnpike byway crosses high mountains and valleys through Monongahela National Forest. The Federal Highway Administration highlights woods, small farms, mountain views and Civil War sites along this National Scenic Byway. Its 180-mile West Virginia corridor runs from Parkersburg to just beyond Bartow. The federal byway page suggests two days to enjoy the route. The eastern mountain section follows a route of switchbacks and loops laid out by Crozet, with the byway guide identifying access to Civil War camps and battlefields.

The original turnpike had a longer ambition: connecting Staunton and the upper Shenandoah Valley with the Ohio River at Parkersburg. Virginia authorized construction funding in 1838, and engineer Claudius Crozet revised his earlier plans for the mountain crossing. Toll houses collected payment from local and through traffic. During the Civil War, early campaigns sought control of the road and the nearby Baltimore and Ohio Railroad. As railroads expanded, through traffic became less important; in the 1920s, the state paved many roads for automobiles while retaining sections of the turnpike.

Drive east from Parkersburg on WV 47 to Linn, then follow US 33 through Weston and Buckhannon to Elkins. US 250 continues southeast through Beverly and Huttonsville, crosses Cheat Mountain and reaches Bartow on the East Fork Greenbrier River. The old turnpike crossed White Top, but modern US 250 skirts the knob beside Shavers Fork.

moments.title: Beverly
moments.text: The turnpike reached Beverly in 1841, and the town grew rapidly as a center of transport and trade. During the Civil War, both armies occupied it at different times, using buildings as hospitals and quarters. Beverly had served as county seat since 1790, but lost that role to Elkins in 1899 as the railroad and timbering center developed. The transfer of the county seat followed multiple referendums and court judgments; armed groups mobilized in both towns, but bloodshed was averted. The town became a historic district in 1980, and a number of its historic structures have been restored.

moments.title: Cheat Summit Fort
moments.text: Cheat Summit Fort stood above the old turnpike on White Top, guarding the approach to the Tygart Valley. Construction began in July 1861. The camp account records snow on August 13 and horses freezing to death in mid-September during its first year of occupation. Mountain weather and strategic changes contributed to its abandonment in April 1862. A cemetery lay south of the fort; after the war, all bodies were exhumed, with many reburied at the national cemetery in Grafton. Depressions from the graves remain visible, marking the former burial ground.

moments.title: Camp Allegheny
moments.text: Confederate troops occupied Allegheny Mountain’s summit pass to defend the turnpike and its approach to the Shenandoah Valley. On December 13, 1861, Union troops attacked in two columns. Difficult terrain delayed the second column until the first had withdrawn, preventing the planned support. The Union attack failed, and the Confederate force remained through winter. Losses through the mountain winter and the difficulty of supplying the remote post contributed to the decision to abandon it in April 1862. The historic district includes earthworks, a cemetery, and the sites of huts, a church and the Yeager farmstead.
